title: What a Company Is and How It Is Formed
summary: The meaning of a company, its separate legal identity, and the four stages of formation in Nigeria, with a note on the law as it stands today.

p: A company is an artificial person created by law to carry on business. It has its own legal identity, separate from its owners, who are called shareholders (or members). It has perpetual succession: it continues even when shareholders die or change. It can own property, make contracts, sue and be sued in its own name.

Formation of a company means registering it with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) in Nigeria and doing everything the law requires so that it becomes a legal person able to begin business. The main law is the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA).

sections.h: The four stages in the textbook
p: A. Promotion. The idea is born. The promoters find a business opportunity, arrange the capital, hire lawyers and accountants and prepare the documents.

B. Incorporation (registration). The company is registered with the CAC. The documents usually submitted are the Memorandum and Articles of Association, the application form (CAC 1.1), a statement of share capital and the fees. When the CAC approves, it issues the Certificate of Incorporation, and the company becomes a legal entity.
C. Capital subscription. For a public company: the company issues a prospectus inviting the public to buy shares until the required minimum capital is raised.
D. Commencement of business. The textbook says a public company must obtain a Certificate of Commencement of Business and a private company can begin at once after incorporation.

sections.h: A note on the law today
p: The lesson note follows the older law. Under CAMA 2020, the certificate of incorporation is the main proof that the company exists; many current guides no longer list a separate certificate of commencement. If your teacher or exam question asks for the four stages, write them as in the textbook and say 'under the older law' where needed, and check the latest CAC guidance for real registrations.

Separate legal identity. Limited liability: shareholders lose at most what they invested in shares. Perpetual succession. Ability to raise large capital, especially for public companies. Easy transfer of shares (in public companies).

title: The Memorandum, the Articles and the Types of Company
summary: The key documents used in formation and the types of company: private, public, guarantee and unlimited.

p: It defines the company's relationship with the outside world. It contains the company's name; its registered office; its objects (what it will do); the liability of members; and the share capital structure.
They are the company's internal rules: how directors are appointed; how meetings are held and votes counted; how dividends are paid; how shares may be transferred.

Certificate of Incorporation: issued by the CAC, confirms that the company legally exists. Prospectus: a public company's invitation to the public to buy its shares, giving details of the business, the management and the financial forecasts.

title: Private Companies
summary: The meaning, features, advantages and disadvantages of private companies, with what CAMA 2020 changed.

p: A private company restricts the transfer of its shares and does not invite the public to buy shares. It is often owned by a family or a small group. Its name ends with 'Limited' (Ltd).

Members: minimum 2 and maximum 50. No public offer of shares or debentures. Shares cannot be freely transferred; approval is needed. A minimum share capital is required (the note gives ₦100,000). Fewer legal formalities and a quick registration. It can start business at once after incorporation. Little public disclosure of its accounts.

The Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 made important changes. A private company can now be formed by one person (a single-member company), so the old minimum of two members no longer applies to private companies. The minimum issued share capital is ₦100,000 for a private company. I could not confirm the 'maximum of 50 members' for private companies under the new law, so treat it as the older rule, and check the Act or a current CAC notice. In an examination, write the figure your teacher or syllabus uses.
The owners keep control. Quick decisions. Lower cost of formation. Confidentiality: its affairs are not published widely.
Limited access to capital (it cannot sell shares to the public). Shares are hard to sell or transfer. The owners carry more of the risk. Its growth is limited by what the owners can raise.

Dangote Industries Limited and many family businesses and start-ups. Note: some companies in the Dangote group (such as Dangote Cement Plc) are public companies listed on the stock exchange; the parent is private.

title: Public Companies and the Differences from Private Companies
summary: Features of public companies, a comparison table with private companies, similarities, advantages and disadvantages and a worked scenario.

p: A public company may invite the public to buy its shares and debentures and may be listed on a stock exchange. It has more legal duties and can raise much more capital. Its name ends with 'Plc' (Public Limited Company).

Members: at least two under CAMA 2020 (the lesson note gives seven, which was the older rule) and no maximum. It can offer shares to the public. Shares can be freely transferred. Accounts must be published. It can be listed. It is closely regulated by the CAC, the SEC and the stock exchange. The note says a certificate of commencement is needed; see the previous unit.
Study the table. The numbers in brackets are the lesson note's older figures.

Both are legal persons. Both must be registered with the CAC. Both can own property and sue or be sued. Both give shareholders limited liability. (A public company is the only one that may sell shares to the public.)
Can raise a large amount of capital. Public recognition and credibility. Shares are easy to buy and sell. Broad ownership helps expansion.
Heavy regulation and cost. Sensitive information must be published. Slower decisions because many people have a say.

Seven people want to start a business and raise funds by selling shares to the public. They should form a public company (Plc), because only a public company can invite the public to buy shares. They will need a prospectus approved by the SEC, and they must obey the disclosure rules.

title: Quoted and Unquoted Companies
summary: The meaning, features, differences, advantages and disadvantages of quoted and unquoted companies, with examples.

p: A quoted company is a public company whose shares are listed and traded on a recognised stock exchange, such as the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX). It has met the exchange's listing rules, and its shares are owned by many members of the public.

Shares are traded publicly. Many shareholders. High disclosure: regular published reports. Regulated by the SEC and the NGX. High liquidity: shares are easy to sell. The market value of the company is known to everybody.
An unquoted company is any private or public company whose shares are not listed on any stock exchange. Its shares are not traded in the open market. Ownership is often private or by a small group.

Shares are not traded publicly. Private ownership. Lower disclosure. Low liquidity: shares are harder to sell. Less supervision: they obey the CAC (and the SEC for public ones) but not stock exchange rules.

sections.h: Advantages and disadvantages of being quoted
p: Advantages: access to large capital; better public image; liquidity for shareholders; public confidence; shares can be used for mergers. Disadvantages: strict rules and public scrutiny; high cost of listing and staying listed; effects of market ups and downs; owners lose some control.

Company names change with mergers and restructuring, so check the NGX website for the current list.

title: The Financial System: Institutions and Instruments
summary: The meaning of the financial system and its four parts: institutions, markets, instruments and laws, starting with institutions and instruments.

p: Every modern economy needs a way to move money from people who have more than they need (savers) to people who need money (investors and borrowers). The financial system is the network of institutions, markets, instruments, laws and procedures that makes this possible. It collects savings and channels them into productive investments.
The system has four main parts: financial institutions, financial markets, financial instruments, and financial laws and regulations.

Depository institutions accept deposits and lend: commercial banks, microfinance banks, mortgage banks. Non-depository institutions give financial services without taking deposits: insurance companies, pension fund administrators, investment banks. Regulatory institutions set and enforce the rules: the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC), and others such as PenCom for pensions.

These are contracts or documents used to raise or invest money. Examples: shares (equity); bonds (debt); treasury bills; commercial papers; mutual fund units (investment funds). Each has different risk and return: for example, treasury bills are short-term and low risk; shares are long-term and riskier.

Rules that govern the system, for example the CBN Act, the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA), the Investments and Securities Act (ISA) and the Pension Reform Act. They protect investors, keep the system stable and demand clear information.

title: Financial Markets and the Functions of the Financial System
summary: The money, capital, foreign exchange and derivatives markets, the functions and importance of a sound financial system.

p: Financial markets are places (physical or electronic) where money, shares and bonds are bought and sold. The main types are in the table.

head: Market
What is traded
Time
Examples
rows: Treasury bills, certificates of deposit, commercial papers

p: 1. Mobilisation of savings: encourages saving and makes the money available for investment. 2. Efficient allocation of capital: sends funds to where they are most productive. 3. Facilitating payments: banks and payment systems make trade safe and easy. 4. Risk management: insurance and other tools spread risk. 5. Monitoring and regulation: promotes honest practice and prevents crashes. 6. Economic growth: supports business, trade and infrastructure.

sections.h: Why a sound financial system matters
p: It encourages investment and new ideas. It reduces poverty through financial inclusion (more people can save and borrow safely, for example through mobile money and microfinance). It builds trust in the economy. It makes international trade and currency exchange possible. It supports government policy, for example by selling bonds.

Savers (households, firms) put money in banks, pension funds or buy securities. Financial institutions and markets pass the money on to borrowers (firms, government, individuals) who invest it. Borrowers pay interest, dividends or repay, and savers earn returns.

sections.h: Financial markets compared with financial institutions
p: Financial institutions are organisations (banks, insurers) that stand between savers and borrowers. Financial markets are the places where financial assets are traded. A stockbroking firm is an institution that works in the market.
